newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank sale imperils Austrian coalition government.
newsitem.headline: Bank sale imperils Austrian coalition government.

text.p: Austria's two-party coalition government began the New Year in gloomy mood, bickering over the privatisation of a key bank in a growing row threatening the survival of the year-old administration.

The sale of Austria's second biggest bank, Creditanstalt-Bankverein, has developed into a dogfight between Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party of Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, verging on a fresh government crisis.
Each coalition party is backing a separate bidder to take over the government's 70 percent stake in Creditanstalt as the drawn-out sale enters its seventh year and comes to a head.

Bidders have until Friday to make their final offers, after which Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima could effectively make his decision on the victor, ending Europe's longest-running privatisation.

Vranitzky said on Monday the sale of the bank was the sole responsibility of Klima. But the conservatives have called a special session of parliament for January 14 to discuss the privatisation and may press for a vote likely to divide the coalition further.
"The session is no reason for the postponement of a decision because parliament is not responsible for the sale of Creditanstalt," the chancellor told the news agency APA.

The Social Democrats and People's Party are entering a critical week with both parties holding separate congresses at which they are expected to lay out their increasingly trenchant opinions on how Creditanstalt should be sold.
Senior conservatives have warned the Social Democrat finance minister to tread cautiously and wait until after parliament meets.
"Klima would be well advised to wait so that he does not take any steps he might regret later," People's Party chairman Andreas Khol said last week.
Khol added that he did not foresee another coalition collapse. But political analysts said this depended on whether the Social Democrats heeded his warning.

Chamber of Economy general-secretary Guenther Stummvoll also cautioned Klima to bide his time. "The economy depends on stable government and anything else unsettles investors and just weakens Austria's economic position," Stummvoll said.
The Social Democrats back a bid for Creditanstalt from Bank Austria, which is effectively controlled by the City of Vienna, dominated by the Social Democrats.
Creditanstalt, bankers to the former Habsburg emperors, has long been considered the preserve of the People's Party, which supports a rival bid by an international group led by insurer EA-Generali.

But the row is not just over the bank sale. It is also a power struggle, exposing the widening ideological gulf between Vranitzky's dominant party -- centre-left but still steeped in Socialist tradition -- and Schuessel's more market-oriented conservatives.

The coalition, in power for 10 years, collapsed in October 1995, when the two parties failed to agree on how to cut a big budget deficit to qualify for European economic and monetary union. A snap election was called in the December.

Although the two parties renewed their partnership early last year, relations have been cool. In the last few weeks, the political temperature fell even further. Now the coalition appears gripped by the same icy chill freezing the Alpine republic.
The bank dispute prompted President Thomas Klestil to call for calm during his New Year address to the nation.
"I have no time for this political power game which is endangering cooperation within the government," he said.
